welcome.title: Make your first master
welcome.body: A short tour shows you how to load a song, shape its sound and save a finished version. You can explore at your own pace.
welcome.privacy_note: Your audio stays on your device. The tour never starts processing or saves audio for you.

steps.title: 1. Add your song
steps.body: Choose an audio file or try the example. Keep your original mix: SlimeyBeats prepares a separate preview and preserves existing exports.
steps.detail: A mix is the whole song. A stem is one part, such as vocals or drums. Start in Mastering for a finished mix, or Studio when you want to edit individual parts.

steps.title: 2. Understand your mix
steps.body: Analyze measures loudness, peaks and tonal balance. It does not change the audio. A measurement is a clue to explore, not a grade for your music.
steps.detail: LUFS describes perceived average loudness. True peak estimates the highest reconstructed signal level. Neither tells you whether a song is enjoyable or needs a particular change.

steps.title: 3. Prepare a master
steps.body: Choose a sound profile and a loudness direction, then Master. This creates a preview. You can change your mind and re-master before exporting.
steps.detail: Profiles are editable starting points. Gentler loudness settings preserve more room for transients; louder settings can reduce dynamics. Advanced controls reveal precise targets and processing options without resetting your choices.

steps.title: 4. Listen and compare
steps.body: Use A/B to compare the source and the prepared preview. Loudness match helps you compare tone without simply preferring the louder version. Listening volume does not change exports.
steps.detail: In Mastering, A is the original mix and B is the master. In Manual EQ, A is the master before your EQ and B includes your EQ. In Studio, the comparison is between the selected edit's before and after audio.

steps.title: 5. Shape the tone
steps.body: Manual EQ changes the balance of bass, mids and treble. Try a small change while listening. Suggested EQ prepares an optional starting curve; you decide whether to apply it.
steps.detail: Frequency chooses where a band works. Gain boosts or cuts that area. Q chooses how narrow it is. The EQ curve shows the change you apply; the spectrum shows energy in the audio. They use different scales.

steps.title: 6. Save when you are ready
steps.body: Export saves the prepared audio to a file. Mastering and previewing do not export automatically. Choose a format and destination, then keep the result you prefer.
steps.detail: WAV is a useful lossless starting point. Existing exports are preserved with a new name. On the web, your browser manages the download destination. On desktop, mastering and Studio remember their export folders separately.

steps.title: 7. Explore Studio when you need it
steps.body: Studio helps you rebalance aligned stems, clean a voice or repair a small audio problem. Import several stem files or a Suno ZIP together. Start with the names you recognize.
steps.detail: Imported stems must have matching timing, sample rate and channel count. Render pending fader changes before another edit or export. Desktop Save project keeps a working session you can reopen; exporting a mix is a separate action. Model separation and VST3 effects are desktop features.

steps.title: You are ready to explore
steps.body: Help stays available in the bottom-right corner. Replay this tour, look up an unfamiliar term or connect an AI assistant to the desktop app whenever you need it.
steps.detail: Use Basic controls for a clear starting point and Advanced controls when you want more detail. Switching views changes what you see, not the processing settings you already chose.

glossary.description: Finishing a whole mix: adjusting its overall tone, dynamics and final level before saving a delivery file.
Balancing individual parts of a song. Studio stem faders help with this; mastering works on the combined result.
Equalization. Change how much bass, midrange or treble you hear. Small changes are often easier to judge.
Where a sound sits from low bass to high treble. Hertz (Hz) measures cycles per second; 1 kHz is 1,000 Hz.
A change in level, measured in decibels. Positive gain raises a level; negative gain lowers it.
How narrow an EQ band is. Higher Q affects a narrower area; lower Q spreads the change more broadly.
A weighted measure of perceived average loudness. A target is an artistic or delivery choice, not a universal quality score.
An estimate of the highest reconstructed signal level, including peaks between digital samples. The ceiling helps leave delivery headroom.
The contrast between quieter and louder moments. Strong loudness processing can reduce that contrast.
Peak protection that reduces gain when a signal approaches the chosen ceiling. Pushing it harder can change punch and dynamics.
Listening-only level adjustment for a fairer A/B comparison. It does not change your exported file.
A finished song used as an optional tonal guide. Pick a relevant sound; matching its measurements does not guarantee a better master.
One aligned part of a song, such as vocals, drums or bass. Imported parts must share the same duration, sample rate and channels.
Mute leaves a part out of the mix. Solo lets you hear the selected part or parts on their own. Neither deletes the source.
A prepared version you can listen to and change. Export saves that prepared audio; Save project preserves a desktop Studio working session.
An optional local connection that lets a compatible AI client use SlimeyBeats tools. You choose the audio and export folders it may use.

mcp.title: Connect an AI assistant
mcp.body: The desktop companion lets a compatible AI client analyze, prepare and edit audio through local tools. SlimeyBeats does not require an AI account to work on its own.
steps: Use the desktop build with its MCP companion included.
Choose an audio folder for the assistant and a separate folder for its outputs.
Generate a connection example, then add the executable and arguments through your AI client's supported MCP setup.
Reconnect the client. Ask it to analyze a track, explain its suggestions and prepare a preview before you approve an export.
mcp.privacy_note: The MCP server runs locally. Your AI client may send prompts, paths and returned measurements to its model provider; its own privacy rules apply. The browser app does not connect to your desktop automatically.
